Empirical Research Plan  
“Islamic Party Victories, Local Governance, and the Welfare of the Poor and Pious: Evidence from Turkey’s 1994 Municipal Elections”  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
I will use a sharp Regression-Discontinuity Design (RD) based on the Islamic party’s vote-margin in the 1994 municipal elections.  

Rationale  
• In Turkish mayoral races the candidate/party with the largest vote share wins; crossing a zero vote-margin threshold (Islamic party vote share – closest secular opponent vote share) deterministically assigns Islamic control.  
• Close elections (± a few percentage points) are widely viewed as quasi-random because small realizations of turnout shocks, weather, campaign gaffes, etc. drive the outcome.  
• RD delivers local average treatment effects for municipalities that could plausibly have gone either way, directly answering “What is the causal effect of Islamic rule relative to secular rule for otherwise similar municipalities?”  
• A panel of pre- and post-election outcomes allows an “RDiD” (difference-in-differences RD) extension that nets out any pre-existing discontinuities and improves precision.  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable  
TREAT_i = 1 if an Islamic party (predominantly Welfare Party, RP) won the 1994 mayoral election in municipality i; 0 otherwise.  

Running variable  
MARGIN_i = Islamic party vote share – vote share of closest non-Islamic competitor in 1994.  

Control group (counterfactual)  
Municipalities with MARGIN just below 0 (secular victory) within an optimal bandwidth h* around the cutoff.  

Timing / variation  
Treatment starts in 1994 and persists for the full mayoral term (1994-1999). Outcomes are measured yearly; the main contrast is post-94 vs. pre-94 levels among municipalities close to the cutoff.  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff  
Absent treatment, poverty rates, religious schooling, infrastructure spending, etc. would vary smoothly in vote margin.  
Plausibility: vote margin is unlikely to influence these outcomes mechanically; no policy is a deterministic function of margin except via winning.  

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable (no sorting)  
Parties and voters cannot fine-tune the vote share to land just above or below zero.  
Plausibility: Secret balloting, limited ex-ante knowledge of turnout, and contemporaneous reports of limited fraud make precise manipulation hard.  

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA)  
A municipality’s outcomes depend only on its own treatment status, not on neighbors’.  
Plausibility: Some fiscal spillovers exist (e.g., commuters), but Turkish municipal budgets and social programs were largely independent at the time. We will test for spatial spillovers.  

A4. Local common trends (for RDiD)  
Among near-cutoff municipalities, pre-treatment outcome trends are parallel.  
Plausibility: Will be assessed via event-study graphs and placebo RD on pre-1994 outcomes.  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  

T1. Manipulation / fraud around the cutoff  
• McCrary density test of MARGIN.  
• Donut RD (exclude ±0.5 p.p.) to eliminate precinct-level irregularities.  

T2. Pretreatment imbalance in covariates or trends  
• Test continuity in 1991 poverty, 1992 budget size, demographic composition, etc.  
• Include those covariates in “covariate-adjusted RD” to improve precision.  

T3. Differential post-election migration (people moving to Islamic municipalities)  
• Check RD in population inflows; if significant, instrument for “years under Islamic rule” with initial victory (leave-one-out two-stage RD).  
• Use outcomes that are measured per-capita and administrative records not easily affected by short-term migration (e.g., infrastructure kilometers built).  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(rdrobust)      # Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik package
library(lfe)           # For RDiD with FE
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# 1. Load data (assume one CSV with panel outcomes)
df <- read_csv("turkey_municipal_panel.csv")

# 2. Construct key variables
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(treated94 = ifelse(islamic_party_won_1994 == 1, 1, 0),
         margin94  = islamic_vote_share_1994 - secular_runnerup_share_1994,
         post      = ifelse(year >= 1995, 1, 0))      # post-treatment years
         
# 3. Basic sharp RD (cross-section 1998 poverty rate)
rd_out <- rdrobust(y = df$poverty_rate[df$year==1998], 
                   x = df$margin94[df$year==1998],
                   c = 0)
summary(rd_out)

# 4. RDiD specification: municipal & year FE within optimal bandwidth
# Select municipalities inside BW chosen by rdrobust
h_star <- rd_out$bws[1,1]
sample_ids <- df %>% filter(abs(margin94) <= h_star) %>% pull(muni_id) %>% unique()

rddid <- df %>%
  filter(muni_id %in% sample_ids) %>%
  felm(outcome_var ~ treated94*post | muni_id + year | 0 | province_id)

summary(rddid)

# 5. Robustness check 1: McCrary density
rddensity_out <- rddensity(df$margin94)
summary(rddensity_out)

# 6. Robustness check 2: placebo RD on pre-1993 poverty
placebo <- rdrobust(y = df$poverty_rate[df$year==1993], 
                    x = df$margin94[df$year==1993], c = 0)
summary(placebo)
```

Replace `outcome_var` with each socioeconomic or religiosity variable in turn; cluster s.e. at province level.  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

6. EXPECTED RESULTS (PRIOR)  
Theory suggests Islamic parties will:  
• Expand targeted welfare and charity programs (zakāt-style aid), reduce poverty among the pious poor.  
• Steer municipal contracts toward co-religionists but potentially crowd out secular businesses.  
Direction:  
– Poverty rate: −1 to −2 percentage points (from a baseline ≈ 25%).  
– Share of children in religious İmam-Hatip schools: +3 p.p.  
– Municipal investment in water & sanitation (km/capita): +5–10%.  

Net impact on growth may be modest or even positive if governance is efficient, but social outcomes (religious schooling, gender segregation) move in a more conservative direction.  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (1 = satisfied, 0 = doubtful)  
1. No manipulation around cutoff (McCrary & Donut) ………………… 0.8  
2. Covariate balance / continuity in pre-trends ………………………… 0.9  
3. Correct functional form & bandwidth choice ………………………… 0.8  
4. Precise treatment definition & no contamination …………………… 0.9  
5. SUTVA / no spillovers …………………………………………………………… 0.7  
Overall average score ………………………………………………………………… 0.82  

I deem the design credible but will transparently report all diagnostic tests, alternative bandwidths, and placebo checks to bolster confidence in the causal interpretation.
